title: First exchange
verifiedBy: LLM review of the romanization, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A yes/no question moves nothing. Vy iz Moskvý? is the statement Vy iz Moskvý with a question mark on the end — no word is added, no word changes place, and there is no Russian equivalent of English do or are jumping to the front. Out loud the question is carried by a rise in pitch on the word being asked about; on the page the ? is all there is.

This course speaks vy — the polite way of addressing somebody. Russian also has ty, for friends, family and children, and it takes its own set of verb endings; picking between them is a real social judgement, so this level makes it once and always chooses the safe one. The slogan to distrust is "vy is just the plural of ty": vy is BOTH the plural and the polite singular, and it always takes the plural verb form even when it means one person.

vy has three written shapes and the job in the sentence picks one: vy does the acting (Vy studént?), vas is the one acted on (Kak vas zovút? — "how do they call YOU"), vam is the one something is done to (M9). It is exactly the ya / menyá / mne pattern from M1, one person further along.

A word describing how somebody is agrees with WHO IS BEING DESCRIBED: a man writes Ya ustál and a woman writes Ya ustála. It is the subject that decides, not the speaker — asking a woman gives Vy ustáli?, because vy always takes the plural shape. English marks none of this and an English speaker will forget it, which is why it is worth its own rule.

A short answer is Da or Net followed by the whole statement: Net, ya iz Índii. Russian does not have the English half-answer ("No, I'm not") that needs an auxiliary to lean on, so the full sentence is the normal reply and it is easier, not harder.

Kak delá? has no verb and no you in it — it is literally "how [are the] affairs", so it carries no ty/vy marking at all and is safe in either register. The fully polite version adds the person back: Kak u vas delá? Learn Kak delá? as one whole phrase; taking it apart is no use at this level.

Greetings are picked by the time of day and by the register: Zdrávstvuyte for anyone at any hour, Dóbroye útro before about noon. Privét exists and is the friend-and-family greeting that goes with ty — it is not a shorter Zdrávstvuyte, and saying it to a stranger lands the way "hey" would land in a bank.

words.note: The all-purpose polite greeting, good at any hour and to anybody. It is built from the old wish "be in good health", which is why it is so long — and it is the vy-form, so the -te on the end is the same -te that marks every polite verb in this course.

sentences.trap: It is long, and English speakers reach for privét because it is short. privét is the ty-greeting: warm with a friend, wrong with a stranger, and there is no polite short one — Zdrávstvuyte is simply the price of the register.
sentences.sound: ZDRAST-vooy-tye. The first v is not said at all, and in fast speech the whole word collapses to "ZDRAS-tye" — that shortening is normal, but it is never written.

variations.changed: swap the name — the greeting itself never changes for who it is aimed at
on its own, with no name — perfectly complete
swap the greeting for the morning one — same frame, different hour

mistake.why: Not wrong Russian — wrong register. privét goes with ty, and this course addresses people as vy. Said to a stranger it is over-familiar.

sentences.usage: Meeting anybody you are not close to: a shop, an office, a first introduction.
sentences.mnemonic: The -te on the end is the polite ending you will meet on every vy-verb from here on.

words.note: Two words, learned as one greeting. dóbroye is "good" in the shape that goes with a neuter noun, and útro ("morning") is neuter because it ends in -o — so the two endings match. That agreement is a system M1 only hinted at; here it is enough to take the phrase whole.

sentences.trap: It is a greeting, not a description of the morning, and it works only before about noon. After that Russian switches phrase entirely rather than stretching this one.
sentences.sound: DO-bra-ye OO-tra. Only the vowel under the acute keeps its full value in each word: the first o of dóbroye is a real "o", the second flattens to "a", and útro's o does the same — which is why the phrase ends in "-tra" and not "-tro".

variations.changed: a name after a comma, exactly as with Zdrávstvuyte
the greeting plus the question that normally follows it
both greetings together — common, and warmer than either alone

mistake.why: útro is neuter, so its describing word has to be neuter too: dóbroye útro. dóbryy is the masculine shape and belongs to other nouns.

sentences.usage: Any morning greeting, in any register — this one is not marked for ty or vy.
sentences.mnemonic: útro ends in -o and dóbroye ends in -oye: the endings rhyme because they have to.

words.note: The polite "you", used for one person or several, and the only "you" this course writes. Three shapes, picked by the job: vy acts (Vy studént?), vas is acted on (Kak vas zovút?), vam is what something is done to (M9's Vam khólodno?). Russian also has ty for friends and family — a genuinely different word with different verb endings, and choosing it is a social decision this level does not ask you to make.

sentences.trap: Nothing moved. English turns "you are from Moscow" into "are you from Moscow" by swapping two words; Russian leaves the sentence exactly as it was and lets the voice do the asking.
sentences.sound: vy eez mask-VY. The pitch climbs on Moskvý and falls away after it — that rise is the whole question, and it is what the ? stands in for.

variations.changed: swap what is being asked about — the frame is just a statement with a question mark
swap the place, and the iz-shape changes with it: Moskvý → Índii
a name instead of vy — the question still moves nothing

mistake.why: The English swap, imported. Russian asks with the words exactly where the statement left them: Vy iz Moskvý?

sentences.usage: Asking a stranger where they are from — the natural second line after a name.
sentences.mnemonic: The question mark does all the work. Nothing else has to.

words.note: "No", and it stands alone or opens a full answer. It has a second job Russian uses constantly — "there isn't any", as in Zdes' net moloká — but that job changes the ending of whatever is missing, so this level leaves it alone and keeps net as the plain answer.

sentences.trap: English answers with a fragment — "No, I'm not" — leaning on an auxiliary. Russian has no auxiliary to lean on, so the answer is the whole sentence: Net, ya iz Índii.
sentences.sound: nyet ya eez EEN-dee-ee. This course spells the word net, with a plain e, and it is still said "nyet": a plain e after a consonant softens that consonant, every time, and here that softening is the whole difference between "net" and "nyet".

variations.changed: the other answer to the same question — Da, then the statement
swap the place — the answer frame does not move
answer about somebody else — still no verb anywhere in the sentence

mistake.why: There is nothing for ne to hang on. Russian finishes the answer: Net, ya iz Índii.

sentences.usage: Correcting a guess about you, politely and in full.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian cannot answer in half a sentence, so it answers in a whole one.

words.note: "How" — and Russian asks for a name with "how", not with "what": Kak vas zovút? is "how do they call you?". The same word opens Kak delá?, where it is asking after the state of things.

"They call" — the verb inside M1's Menyá zovút, here on its own. Nobody in particular is doing the calling; Russian uses this bare they-form the way English uses "they say" or a passive. Swap the person in front of it and the verb does not move: menyá zovút, vas zovút.

sentences.trap: Chto vas zovút? is the word-for-word English question and it is wrong. The Russian question word here is Kak.
sentences.sound: kak vas za-VOOT. The pitch rises on zovút — it is a question, and no word was added to make it one.

variations.changed: vas → yeyó: ask about a third person, and zovút still does not move
the answer to it — the same verb with menyá in front
a name in front, set off by a comma, exactly as English does it

mistake.why: Russian asks how you are called, not what. Kak vas zovút?

sentences.usage: Asking a stranger's name — the polite form, and the only one this course writes.
sentences.mnemonic: Russian does not ask what your name is; it asks how people call you.

words.note: Two words taken whole. delá is "affairs, matters" and there is no verb and no "you" anywhere in the phrase — which is exactly why it is safe in either register: it never has to choose between ty and vy. The fuller, more careful version puts the person back in: Kak u vas delá?

sentences.trap: It is not "how are you" and does not ask after your health. It asks how things are going, and the expected answer is a word about the state of affairs, not about your feelings.
sentences.sound: kak dye-LA. The acute on delá says the stress is on the last syllable, and the pitch rises there too — the whole question is in that rise.

variations.changed: a name in front of it, the usual way of aiming the question
the name after instead of before — both orders are ordinary
the greeting and the question together, which is how they normally arrive

mistake.why: There is no room for vy in this phrase: it is Kak delá?, or the fuller Kak u vas delá?, and nothing in between.

sentences.usage: The standard follow-up to a greeting. With somebody you have only just met, Kak u vas delá? is the safer choice.
sentences.mnemonic: No verb, no you — which is why nobody can say it at the wrong level of politeness.

words.note: The all-purpose "fine". On its own it answers Kak delá?; in front of a verb it means "well" (Ya khoroshó chitáyu, "I read well"); and as a reply on its own it can also mean "all right, agreed".
"Thank you", one word, and it never changes for who is being thanked. It comes from an old "God save you", which is why it looks nothing like anything else in the language.

sentences.trap: Russian answers Kak delá? with a word about the state of things, not with an adjective about you. Ya khoróshiy would say that you are a good person.
sentences.sound: kha-ra-SHO spa-SEE-ba. The kh is one sound, not a k followed by an h — a raspy h made further back than the English one; and two of khoroshó's three o's are unstressed, so they come out as "a".

variations.changed: the answer alone — complete, if a little brisk
the two words the other way round — both orders are ordinary
spasíbo used on its own, thanking somebody by name

mistake.why: The answer needs no "I". Kak delá? asks about things, and Khoroshó answers about things.

sentences.usage: The standard answer to Kak delá?, and the standard thanks for anything.
sentences.mnemonic: Things are fine, not you — so the answer has no "I" in it.

sentences.cue: I am tired (said by a man)

words.note: "Tired", and the shape depends on who is being described: ustál for a man, ustála for a woman, ustáli for more than one person — and also for a single person addressed as vy, because vy always takes the plural. It is the subject that picks the shape, so Vy ustáli? is right even to one man. English says "tired" to everybody and gives you no habit to fall back on.

sentences.trap: The sentence changes with who is saying it. A woman writing Ya ustál has made a real mistake, not a stylistic one — and it is the mistake English speakers make for months, because nothing in their own language ever asks.
sentences.sound: ya oo-STAL, ya oo-STA-la. The acute never leaves that a, so the stress stays put and only the ending moves.

variations.cue: I am tired (said by a woman)
variations.changed: ustál → ustála: the same sentence, said by a woman
the polite you takes the plural shape ustáli, even about one person — and it is a question with nothing moved
about somebody else — the shape follows Anna, not the speaker

mistake.why: vy always takes the plural shape, however many people it means: Vy ustáli?

sentences.usage: Said about yourself after a long day — and it is a normal, unremarkable thing to say in Russian.
sentences.mnemonic: The ending is a small label saying who the sentence is about. Check it before you speak.

words.note: "Yes". Like Net it opens the full answer rather than replacing it, and in speech it also works as a filler at the front of a sentence, roughly "well, …".

sentences.trap: "Yes, I am" cannot be translated: there is no am to end on. Russian says Da and then the sentence, and stopping after Da is abrupt rather than polite.
sentences.sound: da ya stoo-DYENT. Da is short and flat — nothing like the drawn-out English "yeah".

variations.cue: Yes, I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: the answer from a woman — a different word, not a different ending

variations.cue: No, I am a student (a woman correcting the question)
variations.changed: Da → Net, correcting the guess rather than confirming it
answer about somebody else — the frame takes any statement after the comma

mistake.why: There is no verb to confirm with. The answer is Da plus the whole statement: Da, ya studént.

sentences.usage: Confirming a guess about yourself, in full — the ordinary Russian answer.
sentences.mnemonic: Da opens the door; the sentence still has to walk through it.

words.note: Two words that mean "until we meet again" — do is "until" and svidániya is a bent shape of "meeting", bent because do, like iz, changes the word after it. Learn it whole: it is the polite goodbye, and it fits wherever Zdrávstvuyte fitted.

sentences.trap: It is not a formal-only phrase, whatever its length suggests: this is the ordinary goodbye between people on vy terms, and there is no shorter polite one.
sentences.sound: da svee-DA-nee-ya. The do is unstressed and flattens to "da" — it sounds exactly like da, "yes", and only the sentence tells them apart.

variations.changed: swap the name — the phrase never changes
on its own, with no name — complete
thanks and the goodbye together, which is how a shop or an office conversation ends

mistake.why: do bends the word after it, exactly as iz does: svidániye becomes svidániya. The unbent form belongs in a dictionary, not in this phrase.

sentences.usage: Leaving anybody you are on vy terms with — a shop, an office, a first meeting.
sentences.mnemonic: Not "goodbye" but "until the meeting" — Russian says farewell by pointing at the next time.

comprehensionPool.cue: Yes, I am a student (a woman speaking)
Yes, very nice to meet you
